Title: Adjuvant larotrectinib in a resected secretory carcinoma-like lung adenocarcinoma harboring EML4-NTRK3 fusion: case report
PMID: 100946
Authors: Vladmir Cláudio Cordeiro de Lima, Breno Jeha Araujo, Felipe D’ Almeida Costa, Beatriz Fuga Rossi Teixeira, Andre Luiz Cicilini, Carolina de Bustamante Fernandes, Juliana Folador Morellato, Rodrigo Dienstmann, Mariana Tosello Laloni

Abstract
Secretory carcinoma of the lung is an exceptionally rare salivary gland-type malignancy, typically associated with NTRK fusions. We report a 71-year-old woman with pulmonary stage IIIA adenocarcinoma having salivary gland differentiation and solid-cribriform architecture, confirmed by S100 and Pan-TRK immunohistochemistry. Broad DNA and RNA next-generation sequencing identified an EML4-NTRK3 fusion. After adjuvant chemotherapy, maintenance larotrectinib was initiated based on proven TRK inhibitor efficacy in metastatic NTRK-fusion tumors and emerging evidence for targeted therapy benefit in driver-positive early stage lung adenocarcinoma. Our findings demonstrate the value of molecular pathology in the diagnostic journey of pulmonary malignancies, guiding rare fusion detection and supporting therapeutic decisions based on rare fusions in early stage disease.

Case Report
A 71-year-old white woman, psychologist, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score of 0, a 20 pack-year smoking history (abstinent for 6 y), and controlled dyslipidemia (on statin therapy) had a history of stage IIIC luminal breast cancer in 2019 (stage pT2pN3aM0). She underwent adjuvant chemotherapy with dose-dense doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide for 4 cycles and weekly paclitaxel for 12 weeks, followed by radiotherapy and endocrine therapy with anastrozole since 2020 (planned for 10 y), with no recurrence to date. She had two sisters diagnosed with breast cancer but tested negative for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome on germline testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2.
During breast cancer follow-up in September 2024, a previously stable 10-mm right lower lobe (RLL) pulmonary nodule demonstrated interval growth to 15 mm and increased FDG uptake (SUVmax 9.3) on positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) compared with prior imaging. Figure 1A summarizes the patient diagnostic and therapeutic journey.
In November 2024, she underwent robotic-assisted surgical resection of the pulmonary lesion and mediastinal lymphadenectomy. Histopathology revealed a 1.8 × 0.6 cm carcinoma with solid cribriform and microcystic architecture, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and intraluminal secretions, strongly resembling secretory carcinoma of the salivary gland. Focally, there were also areas of micropapillary and complex gland formations. Both lymphovascular invasion and nodal metastases (stations 7 and 9) without capsular extravasation were documented, with final pathologic stage pT1cpN2bM0 (stage IIIA).
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) supported the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma with areas resembling secretory carcinoma of salivary gland origin, revealing focal S100 and nuclear and cytoplasmic Pan-TRK expression (Fig. 1B), with concomitant diffuse TTF1 positivity and mammaglobin negativity. Given secretory features and positive Pan-TRK expression, broad next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed using the GS Infinity panel, an in-house validated assay analyzing 700 genes (SureSelect Agilent DNA and RNA panels), covering mutations, copy number alterations, fusions, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability (MSI). Sequencing identified an EML4-NTRK3 fusion (exon 2–exon 14), as illustrated in Figure 2, with low mutational burden (tumor mutational burden < 10 mut/Mb), mismatch repair proficient (pMMR). In addition, the tumor had PD-L1 expression tumor proportion score equals 20% (antibody 22C3).
Despite the negative hereditary breast and ovarian cancer panel, a larger germline NGS panel was pursued, identifying a heterozygous variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in the RECQL4 gene (c.736A>C; p.Ser246Arg).
The patient completed four cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy (carboplatin area under the curve 5 + paclitaxel 200 mg/m2 every 3 wk) in February 2025. A follow-up PET-CT and brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed no evidence of disease.
Three weeks after completing chemotherapy, the patient started treatment with larotrectinib, 100 mg, twice daily. After 1 week, she developed dizziness and tinnitus, prompting a dose reduction to 100 mg once daily. The patient remains disease free in examinations performed in June 2025. The plan is to continue larotrectinib for 2 years, with imaging reassessment scheduled every 12 weeks.
